opening.say: Picture a basketball leaving a player's hand on a jump shot, heading toward a hoop ten feet up in the air.
Once the ball lets go, nobody touches it again. Whatever happens next, gravity is the only thing still pulling on it.
So we can describe the whole flight with a short formula for the ball's height at each moment in time.

more.say: Take a ball released at two meters high, moving upward at seven meters per second. We can track its height from that single moment.
Right at release, time is zero, so height is just the starting two meters. Then the other two terms begin to push and pull.
The upward speed lifts it, the gravity term drags it down, and together they decide how the height changes second by second.

plan.setup: Watch where the ball goes after it leaves the hand.
plan.narration: [[ball-leaves]]The ball leaves the hand moving up and forward. [[arc-traces]]Its path bends into an arc, a parabola. [[peak-marks]]At the top, the upward speed hits zero for an instant. [[fall-down]]Then gravity wins and the ball drops. [[swish]]Aim it just right, and it drops through the hoop.
plan.plan:
ball-leaves: a ball at release height h_0 leaves a hand, with a faint arrow showing its upward and forward velocity.
arc-traces: the path h(t) draws itself as a smooth downward-opening parabola; the curve equals h_0 plus v t minus four point nine t squared.
peak-marks: a dot pins the highest point of the curve; a flat horizontal tangent shows vertical speed is zero there.
fall-down: the ball slides down the right side of the arc, with a downward gravity arrow staying the same size the whole way.
swish: the curve passes through a hoop ten feet up and the ball drops through the net.
plan.close: Why does the ball slow down on the way up?
